lesson.title: Flipped Through the Origin: Odd Symmetry and the All-Sine Series
lesson.summary: A waveform has odd symmetry when f(-t) equals negative f(t), a 180 degree rotation about the origin, and that guarantees the Fourier series has no DC term and no cosine terms at all, only sines.
lesson.body:
The sine function is the standard example of an odd function: sin(-omega t) = -sin(omega t). A periodic waveform has odd symmetry when the whole waveform obeys the same rule about a chosen origin t = 0: rotating the graph 180 degrees about the point (0, 0) lands it exactly back on itself. Put another way, whatever the waveform does just after t = 0, it does the exact photographic negative, flipped in both time and amplitude, just before t = 0.

This has two consequences for the Fourier series. First, a0 = (1/T) times the integral of f(t) over one period; for an odd function integrated over symmetric limits, the positive-time contribution and the negative-time contribution are exact opposites, so they cancel completely and a0 = 0. Second, an = (2/T) times the integral of f(t) cos(n omega0 t); since f(t) is odd and cosine is even, their product is odd times even, which is odd, and again the integral over symmetric limits vanishes. So for any odd waveform, a0 = 0 and every an = 0. Only the bn, sine, terms can survive.

Here is a fully worked example, using the same square wave introduced in the Harmonic Content chapter, now placed so that t = 0 falls exactly at a transition: f(t) = A for 0 < t < T/2, and f(t) = -A for -T/2 < t < 0. Check the symmetry directly: for t between 0 and T/2, -t falls between -T/2 and 0, where f equals -A; and -f(t) at that same t is also -A, since f(t) = A there. So f(-t) = -f(t): odd symmetry confirmed. Carrying out the integral for bn gives bn = 4A / (n pi) for every odd n, and 0 for every even n, with a0 = 0 and every an = 0, exactly as odd symmetry predicts. For the 10 V peak, 1 kHz version used earlier, that reconstructs as f(t) = (4A/pi)[sin(omega0 t) + (1/3) sin(3 omega0 t) + (1/5) sin(5 omega0 t) + ...], with fundamental 12.73 V, third harmonic 4.24 V, fifth harmonic 2.55 V, and zero cosine content anywhere. This is the same square wave from the Harmonic Content chapter; now you can see why it turned out to have only sine terms. Its odd symmetry guaranteed that outcome before a single integral was computed.

Recognizing odd symmetry by eye is a genuine shortcut in practice: once you have confirmed f(-t) = -f(t), you know immediately that a0 and every an are zero, cutting the remaining Fourier series work roughly in half. It is the mirror companion to the even symmetry test from the previous chapter, and the next chapter adds a third, independent test that looks not at a mirror image but at what happens when you shift the waveform by half a period.
